To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
p53-deficient mouse embryonic fibroblasts with dysfunctional telomeres undergo prolonged G2, bypass mitosis, and enter a second S phase, resulting in whole-genomic duplication and tetraploization.
p53-deficient human cells with dysfunctional telomeres bypass mitosis and enter a second S phase, resulting in whole-genomes reduplication and formation of tetraploid cells.
persistent DNA damage induces bypass of mitosis and tetraploidization.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms that regulate the cell cycle, in particular, mitotic entry, mitotic exit, and cell division.
the molecular basis for the induction of aneuploids and polyploids in cancer.
the molecular mechanisms of tetraploid formation and how it relates to tumorigenesis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
telomere dysfunction induces tetraploidization via prolonged G2 arrest, bypass of mitosis, and re-entry into S phase.
telomere dysfunction induces bypass of mitosis and tetraploization in p53-defective cells.
the induction of tetra-ploidy by persistent telomere damage in p53-defective cells is a novel mechanism of tumorigen-esis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

telomere dysfunction induces tetraploidy in p53-defective cells through persistent ATM/ATR activation, which inhibits Cdk1 and results in a prolonged G2 phase, followed by a second S phase and tetraploidity.
persistent telomere damage can induce a tetraploidization pathway that is mediated by ATM/ATR, Chk1/2 and Cdk1 inhibition.
persistent DNA damage induced by telomere dysfunction results in tetraploidization.
The main takeaway from our work is that
telomere dysfunction is an inducer of tetraploidity in cancer cells.
persistent telomere damage can induce tetraploidy in the absence of mitosis.
persistent telomere damage can induce tetraploidy in a cell cycle-independent manner, which is likely to be a common mechanism for the induction and maintenance of tetraploids in cancer.
